speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of all Canadians, Members of the House, and British compatriots, I would like to extend a most sincere welcome to the Right Hon. Margaret Thatcher during her stay here. As you know, Canadian and British parliamentarians have been exchanging views on world, economic, and social needs for quite some time, and this has always been in the better interest of the Canadian and British parliamentary systems.
Today will be an historic day in Parliament. Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher will be the first British Prime Minister to make a joint address to the House of Commons and the Senate in 25 years. One must recall how another British Prime Minister, Winston Churchill, addressed the Canadian Parliament in this Chamber in a time of global war, aimed at returning the world to global peace.
On this occasion we on this side of the House are particularly glad our Leader and Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will be engaging Mrs. Thatcher in important talks relating to economics, bilateral relations, and ways in which our two nations may work together to bring about world peace.
I know as you know, Madam Speaker, that Mrs. Thatcher will be treated with great civility during her visit to our Parliament. During her four-day visit to Canada, I am sure she will come to know the warmth and hospitality of all Canadians. Having had the honour of being received last spring by Mrs. Thatcher at 10 Downing Street, I can assure the House that the Prime Minister is a most gracious and humble leader of her country.
We are also convinced that Mrs. Thatcher's deliberations with Canadian leaders will be fruitful, meaningful, and will benefit all the Commonwealth.

Madam Speaker, the Government must know by now that the most important policy issue affecting Canadians who live and work in the northern part of Canada is that of taxation. Yet, last week at the Mines Ministers' Conference held in Regina, the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), to the dismay of his provincial counterparts, stated that the Liberal Government had no intention of moderating in the slightest its plan to tax hitherto non-taxed items such as housing and vacation travel allowances.
On the other hand it comes to light that senior officials in the Department of Transport, and CTC commissioners, have been receiving free airline passes from the airlines they are supposed to regulate, and that they have not paid income tax on those travel benefits.
The men and women who work in our northern mines, thereby creating new wealth for Canada, are tiring of the double standard whereby they are to be taxed on every last nickel of deemed benefits when the Liberal "fat cats" in Ottawa get away scot-free.

subsubtopic: BAN ON SMOKING IN AIRCRAFT ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 21 on a question concerning safety for all Canadians who travel as air passengers in this country. On behalf of these Canadians I would like to put forward an additional intervention requesting that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) seriously consider within his Ministry banning smoking on all aircraft in Canada.
On June 20, 1983, 1 raised that question with the Minister's predecessor. As well, the Hon. Member for Welland (Mr. Parent) on June 23 brought this matter to the attention of the House under Standing Order 21 in an attempt to encourage support for the banning of smoking on aircraft. We have a ban on smoking in public places in Canada such as on buses, taxis, and indeed in the House of Commons. This matter is serious enough to warrant the consideration of the Minister of Trans-

September 26, 1983
port to find ways and means to implement a total ban of smoking on aircraft in Canada.

Madam Speaker, the Grit Government should be fully aware by now of the serious economic situation which has developed as a result of the indexation of federal excise taxes on alcohol and tobacco. Automatic increases in these taxes cause future increases at both federal and provincial levels resulting from past increases. This results in a perpetuation of inflation of consumer prices, even if manufacturers were to stop net price increases altogether.
Tobacco is the nation's third most important cash crop. In 1982 it generated total tax revenue of $2.2 billion, of which $1.15 billion flowed into federal coffers. Tobacco manufacturers employed 8,275 Canadians in 1982, and paid more than $216 million in wages and salaries. Employment in the wholesale and retail segments of the industry is estimated at 31,000. The industry is in the top five in terms of capital expenditures, productivity, and absence of work stoppages. Punitive tax policies directly threaten the vitality of this sector of the economy.
Beer, wine, and liquor tax increases are costing that industry more than 37,000 jobs and will result in an increase in the tourism deficit of $700 million in 1983. The President of the Association of Canadian Distillers estimates a loss of 2,000 jobs in that industry alone.
We have seen what punitive taxes did to the oil industry. The pros and cons of smoking and drinking do not enter into this picture. At stake here are thousands of jobs, millions of dollars, and the economic viability of two important sectors of an already fragile economy. When will the Liberals stop using moralistic motives and stop reaping the profits-

subsubtopic: CALL FOR ALL-PARTY MEETING TO DEVISE SOLUTIONS FOR UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a few months ago, as on other occasions, I raised the extremely important matter of unemployment as it affects not only people in Canada today but the future of life in our country. 1 welcome the fact that quite a number of Members have risen and made statements on the same matter. I have in mind, in particular, some of the statements made by my colleagues in this Party. But I want to take this moment to
emphasize that the problem of unemployment and what it may mean for the life of Canada five years or ten years from now is extremely important. It is something with which all of us as a political issue must be concerned.
One suggestion I make is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) consider the possibility of having a meeting of perhaps five or six Liberals, five or six Conservatives, and five or six New Democrats so that we can get together to'come up with statements which will really solve the problem of unemployment today. The future of living in Canada depends on winning this issue. I urge very strongly that we now take active action on it.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF WOMEN AGED 50 TO 65 YEARS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in Canada today we have assistance for those over age 65, we have the spouse's allowance for those between the ages of 60 and 65, and we have the Canada Pension for the disabled under the age of 65, but for thousands of women between the ages of 50 and 65 there is nothing. I submit that this big gap in our social assistance program is a priority item.
Every week women between the ages of 50 and 65 come to me. Some are single who looked after an aging parent or a crippled brother, some are divorcees who were left stranded to raise a family by an uncaring husband, and some are divorced, but all now find it difficult to get work even if their health permits them to work.
My husband left me with three little girls, and instead of going on welfare I scrubbed floors, sold cards, peddled seeds, and did everything I could to keep my children dressed and in school.
Now they are away from home, my health is gone, I have no unemployment insurance, I have no Canada Pension, and I am 60 years of age. Can you help me?
These were the words of a woman who bravely held back her tears when I had to tell her that there is no program in Canada to help her, except welfare. She shuddered at the thought of accepting welfare. This is not the story of just one woman. Thousands of women have similar stories, and they are heartbreaking. In this rich country surely we can provide enough priority to fill this gap in our social assistance program. These women lived in dignity. Surely we are not going to let them die in poverty.

Madam Speaker, I rise to make a statement regarding a report in this weekend's newspapers that the federal Government is ready to approve
September 26, 1983

another $750,000 grant for the controversial Cape Breton coal liquefaction project headed by former Liberal Energy Minister Alastair Gillespie. The Government would be wise to pause here and take stock before going ahead with these grants. To put it mildly, the matter raised quite a furor in the House of Commons for a week the last time the possibility of a grant to Mr. Gillespie and his associates was raised.
The Sharp task force, which was formed on July 7 of this year, is to look into the really difficult matter of conflict of interest guidelines for former Ministers. The Government should wait for its report. It should indeed have looked further into the Gillespie matter and held a special open inquiry.
1 also question the consistency of the policy as reflected by the energy policy and some of the statements made this past weekend by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien). Are we going for coal liquefaction, or are we going to stick with the $8 billion which we are giving for petroleum incentive program grants for the Beaufort Sea and other areas? Or are we going to buy, which would be cheaper for the Canadian consumer, offshore oil from Saudi Arabia or Venezuela? The Government is being inconsistent here. Before it gives this grant, it should take pause.

subsubtopic: SEIZURE OF CLAN FRASER CRESTS AND EMBLEMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on July 15 Douglas Fraser and his wife, American tourists from Georgia, arrived at Canadian customs in Windsor. The purpose of their visit to Canada was to attend a Scottish festival in Orillia, Ontario. Mr. Fraser is the chairman of the Clan Fraser Society of North America. Not being familiar with Canadian customs regulations, they failed to declare $1,200 worth of T-shirts, crests, lapel pins and assorted articles, all designated with Clan Fraser crests which they intended to exhibit and sell at the festival. Rather than acting with understanding and good will, the customs officers seized all the articles and their vehicle, threatened them with jail, and refused to listen to any explanation.
My purpose for raising this on the floor of the House of Commons is this. We are trying to build a tourist industry in Canada. We do that by creating events and attracting tourists to Canada, to Orillia and other parts of this country. All of our efforts go for naught if heavy-handed customs officials at points of entry discourage tourists from coming to Canada by using secret police tactics on innocent people.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 appreciate the fact that the Prime Minister is unable to be in the House at the moment so I will direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister.
On Friday of last week official Government statistics proved beyond a shadow of a doubt the magnitude of the social problems that have been created because of the Government's misguided economic policies. subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY

speechtext:
The House resumed from Friday, November 26, 1982, consideration of the motion of Mrs. Erola that Bill C-12, respecting bankruptcy and insolvency, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
Bankruptcy Act

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make some observations about Bill C-12 before we pass it along to the Standing Committee. This Bill has been around for more than eight years. It has had a variety of Bill numbers. It was first introduced in 1975 as Bill C-60. After introduction and by negotiated agreement it was sent on to the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce. That Committee recommended 139 changes to the Bill. It was withdrawn and resubmitted as Bill S-ll and introduced again in the Senate on March 21, 1978. It did not move forward for debate but was reintroduced as Bill S-14 on February 27, 1979. Again it was introduced in the House on April 16, 1980, and three years and five months after this present session commenced we have it before us again for debate.
The Bill has had about one and a half days of debate, and we now have it again for debate and reference to the Standing Committee. We might ask why this Bill, which is so vital to the conduct of good business practice, has been left on the back burner for so many years. It could be said that the tremendous increase in business and personal bankruptcies over the past five years made the Bill a focal point for an attack on Government economic policies. To put it another way, it was a good debating Bill but could be very embarrassing to the Government. It chose to keep it down the list of legislation.
But why bring it forward now, we might ask? The answer is quite simple: pressure from the business community, a good and valid reason. Business bankruptcies have risen from 3,700 in 1979 to 6,897 in the first eight months of 1983. Farm bankruptcies in that same period in 1979 amounted to 77 for the first eight months and 287 for the first eight months of 1983. The losses suffered were quite substantial-$585 million in 1979 and $1,390 million in that same eight-month period in 1983. If we add to that personal bankruptcies, sometimes called consumer bankruptcies, we see that they increased from 11,670 in the first eight months of 1979 to 18,476 in the January-August period of 1983, an increase of 58 per cent in four years.
The real reason the Bill is being brought forward is the Maislin Transport bankruptcy. Pay cheques were bounced in an operation into which the Government poured several hundred million dollars. The bail-out money did not help; it was just too close to home. Too many Ministers and Fiberal Members were feeling the heat, and now we have the Minister saying that she will amend the Bill to give some priority to wages of employees caught in a bankruptcy. It was only when a large Quebec-based company went under and its employees, friends and creditors put sufficient heat on Quebec Members to cause them to worry about their electoral base that the Bill was given priority and brought forward.
The statistical record is shocking. Just going back four years and picking the January to August period of eight months from 1979 to 1983, there were 77,547 personal bankruptcies and 26,981 business bankruptcies with losses of $4,270 million. That was the 1979 to 1983 period, the January to August eight-month figures. But only when Maislin Transport was in

September 26, 1983
Bankruptcy Act
difficulty, some employees had payroll cheques bounced and the heat was applied to Quebec Members of Parliament, did we see some movement on the Government legislative list. So much for the background and history of the Bill.
I have not mentioned the businesses which have been put into receivership or chose voluntary liquidation. We have no statistics for that group, but 1 have heard figures of from 6,000 to 18,000 per year. I accept the lower figure in the absence of some proof of the higher number. When we see the dimensions of this economic tragedy, we understand why there are almost two million unemployed people in Canada and the gloomy forecast for employment down the road. We cannot eliminate 26,981 businesses and have another 30,000 going into receivership in four years without expecting to have massive job dislocations and personal bankruptcies. You cannot wipe out $4 billion or $5 billion in losses as the result of bankruptcies and probably a similar amount from businesses placed into receivership and not have disastrous waves in the economy.
The human tragedy is the biggest loss. Thousands of entrepreneurs closed their doors forever. Using the full year's comparison for 1979 to 1982, the number of businesses forced to close their doors increased by 91 per cent. In 1982 alone, over the 12-month period, 10,763 businesses were forced to close their doors forever.
Rather than take action to repair the economy, the Government has chosen to throw massive amounts of money at selected companies. To date Canadair has cost the taxpayers of Canada $2 billion. That sum of money is almost equal to the total liabilities of ail the businesses that were declared bankrupt in 1982.
I know we have the commercial Galahads with us who say that only the strong survive or should survive. Others will tell you that the businesses were poorly managed. They will also tell you that most small and medium-sized businesses are undercapitalized. A few go under due to fraud. You may be surprised to learn that in the retail trade more losses are recorded by employee theft than by bankruptcy. I suspect there is a bit of truth in all the excuses or reasons for bankruptcy or receiver-trustee arrangements.
The bankruptcy legislation first passed in 1949 has not kept pace with the times. It was amended once in 1966 and has seen nothing more until this Bill in its various forms was introduced. In the intervening years much has changed in commercial practice. The employees and unsecured creditors have been abused by the major creditors and by autocratic receivers.
We are aware of deals between unethical receivers who dispose of assets at distressed prices through the economic vultures. These vultures are known to the receivers. They offer ready cash for good, saleable merchandise and raw materials. In many cases no competitive bids are received. A lot of arranged sales are made to the detriment of the unsecured creditors. Our objective should be to amend this legislation to see more justice, honesty and equity in these tragedies.
Today in Canada we have the most illogical, ambiguous, contradictory and grossly unfair income tax system of all the western democracies. We have bankruptcy legislation that has gone unamended since 1966. In that period of time our economy has exploded and we have been ravaged by inflation and bankruptcies. Survivors of the current recession are standing with their balance sheets stripped bare of capital assets. If there is a bump of any significance in the current recovery, many of the survivors will join the tens of thousands who have gone under.
Do we find many objectors to any amendments to this legislation? Not many have raised their heads to date, but I am sure there will be some. I note in the April 18 issue of The Financial Times that mention is made of a new Ontario law on liens and there is the comment that it worries the developers. The article states that the new legislation in Ontario that affects the assets of a bankrupt developer changes the rules under which major lenders extend financing. It further comments that it will raise the cost of borrowing for developers. I find that concept of financing rather disgusting. The article states in effect that should a developer become insolvent, the lender who finances the developer must have the assets of the suppliers and the subcontractors free from and unencumbered by liens at his disposal. The lender must have his free ride or he will raise the cost of money to the developer.
The Province of Ontario has moved, quite properly, to give some measure of protection through a lien to subcontractors and suppliers to a developer. One bank commented that this lien protection given by the new act in Ontario is a serious impairment to any lender. This recent change in Ontario legislation is a step in the right direction. It should cause us to look at the plight of the unsecured creditor and employees of a company in bankruptcy or receivership when we consider this legislation.
Many businesses with stripped balance sheets are at the mercy of the receiver-trustee who is petitioned to take over the business that is in difficulty. The receiver can, upon direction of the largest creditor, usually a bank, seize and sell the assets to satisfy the bank's liability. Inventory and good fixed assets are sold at distressed prices. Anything that is left is dispersed to the unsecured creditors. The bank and National Revenue are usually first on the list of those who are secured creditors and receive their outstanding accounts.
The power in the hands of the receiver is awesome. Some unsecured developers have developed a defence against the all-powerful receiver. I can recall a particular instance in my own business: a company ordered several thousands of dollars worth of material from my company. The credit information indicated the customer was in good financial condition. After 45 days passed, we called for our outstanding receivable only to be advised that the cheque was prepared and was awaiting signature. That is a favoured excuse. After 60 days we called again, accepted apologies, and were assured that the cheque would go forward within a week.
We heard a rumble in the trade that suggested our customer had a cash flow problem. We called again and offered to take
September 26, 1983

back some or all of our merchandise. The customer declined and said our cheque was on top of those cheques awaiting signature. Further commercial credit investigation did not indicate any serious financial problem beyond a slow-pay rating. We heard another rumble in the trade, called our customer again and asked if we could borrow back some of our merchandise as we had a large order to fill and did not have enough products on the shelf to fill the order. Our customer agreed to "loan" us our own merchandise and we despatched our truck to bring it to our warehouse. Within 48 hours the company was in receivership. Within 60 hours the receiver called and demanded that we return our merchandise. He fretted, he fumed, he used numerous unparliamentary words and expressions when 1 told him we would not return the merchandise. He quoted me the law, said he would get a court order and force me to return the merchandise and further threatened to bring the sheriff with him and seize the merchandise. The more enraged he became, the more secure I felt. I thold him where to go, how to get there and hung up the phone.
After several more phone calls with threats of court action, I invited him to proceed and said that we were prepared to meet him in court. My position was that he had taken every precaution possible in a normal commercial transaction. We had offered to take back the merchandise to relieve the cash flow problem we heard they were experiencing, albeit unofficially. We know what we did was unlawful. However, after you have been stung a number of times in bankruptcies, you get hardened to a law that is out of date with the realities of the commercial marketplace.
I could tell you more about experiences, Mr. Speaker, such as going to the final meeting of an unsecured creditor to find that I was the only one of more than 300 creditors who turned up. in fact, the meeting was held in the receiver's 12 by 12 office. He laughed when I asked for a statement of the final disposition of accounts. I did not laugh, but he thought it was strange that anyone would show up for the meeting. I was struck by the arrogant, callous and flippant attitude of the receiver. You get more respect from a slot machine. We must see that the unsecured creditors have a security mechanism available to them.
We must amend this legislation as well to protect the employees' wages. We must remove potential conflict of interest between receiver-trustee functions and manager-creditor functions. Unsecured creditors must be kept informed by the receiver-trustee of the amount received on the disposition of assets. More important, they should have some input into the decision to sell or dispose of assets by auction.
I would like to see an amendment put in the statute that would protect the businessman from the Government when that Government is party to his going into bankruptcy. I am sure all of us at one time or another have had a call from a businessman informing us that National Revenue is closing in because he did not remit his employee payroll deductions, income tax, UIC, CPP or whatever. It should be a requirement that those funds be placed in a trust account and not be
Bankruptcy Act
attachable by the bank. That should get the Government out of its preferred position in a bankruptcy. However, I refer to more serious matters.
There are many reasons for bankruptcies. Clarkson Company Limited, the oldest trustee in bankruptcy in Canada, estimates that 70 per cent of all business failures can be attributed to poor management. But what about the case of Mr. Lome Shields, a man who perhaps knows more about the bicycle business than anyone in Canada? Mr. Shields had an excellent business and earned about $400,000 annually in bottom line profits. He was an importer of bicycles who, for market and tariff reasons, decided to begin to manufacture his requirements in Canada. He set up a manufacturing facility, hired about 200 people, and pre-sold a year's production at a profit.
One day, Sir, Mr. Shields had a visit from a dominion customs appraiser named John Peillard who told Lome Shields that he was not a manufacturer of bicycles but was an assembler, and as such that he must pay duty on the imported components he used in his production. Mr. Shields said: "All my competitors import duty free". "No matter," said the dominion customs appraiser, "you are classified as an assembler and therefore you are not entitled to duty-free status; and furthermore, we demand payment of $310,000 duty which we have assessed your company".
Well, Sir, Lome Shields was devastated. He came to Ottawa, he bumped around National Revenue and finally, after numerous trips to the capital, the Minister of National Revenue agreed to see him. Now, the Minister with a smiling, shining face agreed that Mr. Shields had been badly done by. He said he would have the ruling changed right away and Mr. Shields left happy.
About two weeks later, Mr. Shields received a letter from the Minister saying that the Minister was very sorry but he could not change the ruling laid down by his officials, that the $310,000 levy must stand, that he was indeed an assembler and not a manufacturer and National Revenue must have its money now.
What Mr. Shields did not know was that a deal had been struck by the Enterprise Development Board. It had received an application from CCM for another bundle of money to bail it out of another financial mess. The Board turned that application down, but the Minister did not want to see CCM go into bankruptcy because an election was on the horizon. So they cut a deal, as they say in the trade. Somehow they had to get rid of Lome Shields' operation because, as the CCM people said, he had such a share of the market that CCM could not become profitable unless Shields was out of the market and they had his chunk of the market. So a method was found to put Lome Shields to the wall. All this had been cooked up before the dominion customs appraiser came to Lome Shields' place of business. He was only the messenger.
Mr. Shields was petitioned into bankruptcy by his bank. He had paid $230,000 of the $310,000 invoice for the duty to

September 26, 1983
Bankruptcy Act
National Revenue in the sure understanding that the Minister of National Revenue would have the classification of his business changed and the funds paid would be returned. Meanwhile, Mr. Shields' lawyer took the matter to the Tariff Appeal Board. It heard the case about 24 months later.
Mr. Shields and his lawyer had a discussion with the dominion customs appraiser. They questioned the definition of the terms "manufacturer" and "assembler". They asked to see the statute or the regulations that described a manufacturer and an assembler. The customs appraiser told them it was not written in the statute or the regulations but was contained in an interdepartmental memo between Deputy Ministers. In orther words, they had assessed a duty upon Lome Shields for imported components in his product and did not have the statutory or regulatory authority to back it up. They told him that interdepartmental memos were confidential and that he could not see them. The Tariff Board confirmed this fact 24 months later and ordered the return of Mr. Shields' $230,000 duty payment and the cancellation of the $80,000 outstanding balance being demanded by National Revenue.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you about the fairness, justice and equity of the situation, so here is what happened to the major players in this sordid game. Mr. Lome Shields went into bankruptcy and lost everything. The dominion customs appraiser, Mr. John Peillard, was given a lateral promotion and was moved to the electrical section as an appraiser.
The National Revenue officials, the Assistant Deputy Minister and the Deputy Minister to whom Mr. Piellard reported and took direction went on their merry way collecting their rewards as usual, protected from the commercial world they regulate.
The Minister of National Revenue went to his just reward in the other place, where he sits saying even less today than he said when he was a Member of the House of Commons. His face is still smiling and shining, especially when his monthly pay cheque arrives.
Did Mr. Shields, the victim of this undercover crime, have an MP? Mr. Speaker, I see that you are ready to rise. I would ask the indulgence of the House to allow me to continue. I have just a few more words to say, if you would put that question, Sir.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank Hon. Members for their courtesy.
You might ask, Sir, did Mr. Shields, the victim of this undercover crime, have an MP? In this representative democracy, was he represented in Parliament? Did Mr. Shields' MP try to do something or anything for him? Well, yes, he met Mr. Shields at a social function and said: "Sorry, there is nothing I can do for you". There was no measure of justice, equity or fairness that could be applied to the case of Mr. Shields.
What is Mr. Shields' MP doing today? Well, Sir, he is the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kaplan). What happened to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who was the real mover and shaker behind this sordid economic tragedy? Well, he was defeated in the 1979 election, as he should have been.
Oh, yes, what happened to CCM? They were to benefit from the demise of Lome Shields' enterprise. Well, they finally bit the dust after consuming almost half a billion dollars in grants and guarantees over a period of years.
As horrible as all that sounds, Sir, it is a true story. I have to ask myself, should not Lome Shields get some redress? The Government of Canada, through its Ministers and officials, caused a thriving business to go into bankruptcy. Those Ministers and officials knew they did not have the statutory or regulatory authority to levy a tariff bill against him. Regardless, he was put to the wall and thrown into bankruptcy. He was a successful, profitable employer of 200 people, contributing to the GNP and the tax base of the country. Yet through behind-scenes manoeuvring, he was thrown into bankruptcy.
Almost three years from the time Mr. Shields gave the Government a $230,000 cheque, he received a rebate from National Revenue. It went to the receiver to try and pay some of his unsecured creditors.
Again, Mr. Speaker, National Revenue put the knife into Mr. Shields. After using his $230,000 for nearly three years, it did not even pay him interest on the money it illegally took from him. So much for fairness, equity and justice.
I do not know if we can protect people from devious and deceitful public servants. 1 have received a number of painful phone calls recently, and I know other Hon. Members have as well, from retail clothing store owners who told me that a special inspection was being put in place for textile products that they were importing. This was done without warning. Suddenly shipments were being held at the border, demurrage charges were mounting and fall retail sales were curtailed because the Government had only a handful of specially trained people to do the inspections. Had the situation continued much longer, many retailers would have gone bankrupt. As it now stands, many of them will have reduced earnings because of demurrage charges by the carrier of the goods and because of many lost sales. We need some protection from the Government, perhaps in the way of a court injunction or some other device. I hope that we can deal with this aspect at committee. Let us agree to have a full and thorough hearing before the standing committee so that these matters may be aired.
Let me conclude, Sir, by making a plea. People watching the House of Commons proceedings sometimes comment that our proceedings are irrelevant. They do not understand that this House is a debating forum and that it is the nature of a representative democracy that members bring forward their views on a variety of matters offered for debate and state them as forcefully as allowed.
September 26, 1983

One of the hallmarks of a democratic society is the measure of fairness, equity and justice written into its statutes. We have an opportunity to repair a statute that is short on those qualities.
Our economy is improving, but any slight bump or hesitation will cause it to fall back. Investors are looking for marks of confidence, indications that someone is seriously looking at the defects in our economic process. We have an opportunity to place a mark that says we have repaired the inequities in our bankruptcy statute and made it fair, equitable and just so that some of those businesses that find themselves financially strapped may have a reprieve or a second chance. If that is not possible, then the distribution of the assets must be done in such a way as to yield the greatest dollar value for distribution to all the creditors.
I want to thank you, Mr. Speaker, and Members of the House for allowing me to have extra time to place those comments on the record. When the Bill goes to committee I hope we will have wide-ranging hearings so that we may repair some of the inequities that are present in our economy today.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) on his speech. Obviously he draws upon a wealth of personal experience in this area of the law. I look forward to hearing from the Hon. Member in committee. He would obviously strike terror into the heart of any receiver who dared come near any of his constituents. I commend him for the tenacity with which he has approached the question.
The Hon. Member referred to the glaring inequities in the legislation. One of the most glaring inequities, and I am sure he would agree, is the present status of wage earners who are often consigned to the bottom of the totem pole when it comes to distributing the assets of a bankrupt firm. I should like to ask the Hon. Member what the position of his Party is with respect to the establishment in Canada of a wage earner protection fund, an insurance scheme, which would be financed by contributions from employers. I do not mean from small employers of less than six people, but, rather, from large employers. What is the position of the Hon. Member for Burlington and his Party on the establishment of such a wage protection scheme as recommended by the Senate committee and the Landry Commission?

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to make a few comments with respect to this important legislation which, as has been indicated by previous speakers, has been before the House in one form or another for the past eight years. I note that we finally have a reply from the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) about the position his Party takes with respect to the question of the protection of the status of wage earners. The Hon. Member indicated-and other positions on that may be taken by Members of the same Party in the other place, that he does not support the establishment of a wage insurance scheme, as was recommended by all of those who have looked at this issue.
During second reading debate my colleagues have dealt with a number of important issues which arise during any discussion of bankruptcy legislation. The Hon. Member for Kam-loops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) and the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) and others dealt with many of the

September 26, 1983
Bankruptcy Act
key economic questions which arise in this important area of bankruptcy. They have noted, and I reiterate, that there has been an explosion in the granting of credit in Canada, there being some $30 billion outstanding in credit.
The Liberal Government's economic policy has not only failed but has resulted in high interest rates and the collapse of consumer demand. Small businesses have been particularly hard hit by this and the level of bankruptcies in Canada has reached historic high. Last year, for example, bankruptcies left behind some $3.6 billion in debts. As well, in 1982 there were over 40,000 corporate and personal bankruptcies in Canada. Many of these resulted in tragic personal losses to the individuals involved as well as to the communities. In the case of corporations which go bankrupt, the spin-off effect can be devastating to a small community.
I must also comment on what in my view is the serious failure of the Federal Business Development Bank to take a tough but fair look at requests for financing, particularly by small businesses, in these difficult economic times. While the Government is prepared to bail out the big boys, the Domes, the Chryslers and the Maislins, for too many small businesses go under when, with a little bridge financing by the Federal Business Development Bank, they would survive. A restaurant in my constituency of Burnaby is a prime example of this. The Federal Business Development Bank turned the owner down flat but he was able to borrow funds from other sources and, fortunately, his operation is thriving today. Had he not been in the position to borrow elsewhere, he might have gone under. That kind of attitude on the part of the FBDB in the face of Government largesse to the big corporations is unacceptable.
Credit is granted far too easily today. Many individuals have accumulated debts which they cannot possibly repay, whether they be credit card or other forms of consumer debt. The advertising which is used to promote credit is, in many instances, overwhelming, and when an individual loses his job he is often completely stranded.
These are some of the serious questions which arise in this difficult area of bankruptcy. I look forward to a careful study of the key issues which arise as a result of the tabling of the legislation. I believe that the committee hearings must be comprehensive and must afford an opportunity to all individuals to make representations as to the impact of this legislation.
At the same time I would note that clearly the time to move forward on changes to this area of the law is now. We have waited far too long for amendments to this archaic legislation. Certainly, as long as the Government is prepared to respond sensibly and with some concern, particularly in one or two of the areas 1 will be touching upon shortly, I am confident that finally we will see some changes in this area of the law.
By far the most contentious provision of this legislation is the provisions which deal with the priority which is to be accorded to workers who are owed money in the event of a bankruptcy. This is the issue, Mr. Speaker, which has dominated all of the discussions surrounding this legislation from
the time that the First Bill, Bill C-60, was tabled in this House in 1975. This Bill was tabled in response to the Tasse report, which was issued by the Government in 1970. This report very clearly documented that there are major flaws in bankruptcy legislation as it presently exists.
The Senate committee which looked into the provisions and studied the subject matter of Bill C-60 heard representations from a broad cross-section of the community. Following its study, it came to the conclusion that the recommendations of the Government in Bill C-60 were fundamentally flawed. That Bill recommended a $2,000 super priority for wage earners over and above secured and preferred creditors. The Senate committee unanimously rejected that approach and, in my view, its reasons for doing so are as sound today as they were when it came forward with its report in 1978.
I would note that again in 1980, following the tabling by the Government of Bill C-12, the Senate committee studied the whole question and paid particular attention to the arguments which had been made in support of a super priority. 1 note that the Bill which is now before the House, however, contains no super priority whatsoever for wage earners. Rather, it would place wage earners in the same category in which they are presently placed. The only change would be an increase in the overall amount. However, in virtually all instances that would have no impact whatsoever. Obviously changes must be made and made very soon, because far too many working people are left out when it comes to a bankruptcy or receivership.
The two fundamental approaches in this area are either super priority or the establishment of a wage earners' insurance fund. The Conservative Party has indicated that it supports a super priority and is opposed to the establishment of a wage earners' insurance fund, despite the evidence before the Senate committee and despite the unanimous report of the Landry Commission which very carefully examined this whole area.
Before looking at the relative merits of those two solutions, Mr. Speaker, I might indicate the dimensions of this problem. It is very easy to talk in global terms about the devastating impact of a bankruptcy on working men and women in terms of their inability to continue to pay their rent, buy food and pay for the ongoing expenses which they face in these difficult times. This point was dramatically driven home to me when I received a letter from one of my constituents, a young man who graduated from Burnaby Central Senior High School in 1982. I can do no better, Mr. Speaker, that quote from the letter which he sent to me, which very eloquently points to the difficulties facing working people in this area. He said the following:
During the summer months I entered the work force in hopes of obtaining sufficient funds to attend Simon Fraser University this spring semester. I was able to receive employment with Truwall Construction (Alberta) Limited of Calgary. Truwall met with some financial difficulties and was forced into receivership. I obviously felt bad for all those involved, but felt that reimbursement of wages to employees would most definitely be top priority. Today after several months of correspondence-
That was with the employment standards people in the Alberta employment standards branch.
September 26, 1983

-1 was rudely awakened to the fact that it was not me, the employee, whose concerns were met with first, but those of the Royal Bank of Canada.
1 find this to be a gross injustice to all those employees, including myself, who were affected in this manner.
I ask you, my Parliamentary representative, to assist me with this matter and to explain to me why those least able to defend themselves are hardest hit.
My hopes of paying my own way through university, at least for this year, are futile. My only recourse is to burden my more than willing parents with this.
Please consider my complaint.
The letter is signed by Brad Gilmour of Amberwood Place in Burnaby, British Columbia. What more graphic evidence does the Government need of the importance to move quickly to ensure a realistic priority for working people?
As well, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), has been most diligent in pursuing the question of the rights of working men and women at the White Farm Equipment Company of Canada in Brantford, Ontario. I would note that if this company were forced into bankruptcy, the employees there stand to lose over $6 million in fringe benefits and severance pay. We are talking here, Mr. Speaker, of over 1,000 employees. Imagine the devastating impact this would have not only on the employees and their families but on the entire community of Brantford, which is so dependent on this major employer. Once again I want to commend my colleague, the Hon. Member for Brant, for his diligence in pursuing efforts to keep this company alive and thriving in order that this bankruptcy will not in fact have this impact.
There are many other examples of bankruptcies in other parts of Canada, including the Maislin bankruptcy, where workers have been left completely out in the cold. The banks have swooped in and taken what assets do remain and have left the employees with nothing. In January of 1982 four building supply companies which were owned by a Vancouver chartered accountant were put into receivership when they could not keep up with their loan payments. The companies had stores in eight different British Columbia communities, many of them small communities. Most of their employees were laid off without any notice whatsoever. Because the companies filed for bankruptcy and the secured creditors swooped in, these employees were once again denied any back pay whatsoever.
As 1 have indicated, the problem is a real one. It is a growing one at a time of economic crisis and of record bankruptcies in this country.
The question is, then, having recognized the depth of this problem, what is the appropriate response to it? I have noted that there are effectively two alternatives: super priority, as proposed initially in Bill C-60, and the establishment of a wage insurance scheme.
The Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce unanimously rejected the proposal for super priority. I would like to outline its reasons for rejecting this proposal. 1 remind Hon. Members of this House and those persons who are viewing these proceedings today that this was a unanimous report with both Conservative and Liberal senators concurring strongly. The report stated that super priority, as proposed in Bill C-60, does not achieve the objectives of certainty of payment to the wage earner; promptness of payment to the
Bankruptcy Act
wage earner; ease and simplicity of administration; and the maintenance of the ability of a borrower to obtain financing for his business operations.
I will deal briefly with each of these points because on each count, Mr. Speaker, super priority does not answer the needs of working men and women. First with respect to certainty of payment to the wage earner, as the committee indicated there is no certainty whatsoever that wages owing by the bankrupt will be paid. In many instances, the assets of the bankrupt will be completely insufficient even to meet the top priority of wages, and often sophisticated lenders might stipulate that their loans will be made to an associated holding company which owns all of the valuable assets, once again leaving workers out in the cold, even in the face of a super priority.
A second and very important point is that the Committee noted that there is no guarantee whatsoever that the payment to the wage earner will be made promptly. Surely Hon. Members of this House will recognize the importance of promptness in making such payments because wage earners must pay their bills on a day to day basis and cannot afford to have significant delays-weeks, months, possibly even longer-in the payment of their claims. So once again, even though they may have super priority on paper, they will, in practice, not receive the funds for many, many months in many instances. Often the assets of the bankrupt company will not be readily convertible into cash and the lender might be very reluctant to borrow money.
Yet another difficulty with the concept of super priority which the Conservative Party supports is the serious difficulties in administration of this proposal. Most significant would be allocation of the burden of this super priority among the secured creditors of the bankrupt. The courts would be clogged with bitter disputes over the relative burden to be shared by creditors, and while the courts are clogged and lawyers are arguing, workers will receive nothing whatsoever.
Finally, I would note that super priority may very well very impair or reduce the credit which is available in a labourintensive industry. Surely this cannot be an objective which would be sought by Members of the House. The final conclusion of the Senate Committee was that super priority is not the proper method for granting wage earners the protection they deserve.
In the face of that conclusion it is most surprising to hear that the Conservative Party and apparently the new Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) are prepared to accept a proposal for super priority which has been soundly rejected by a detailed study of the Senate Committee.
Not only did the Senate Committee look into this question, but following the Senate report the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs established a special committee to examine this whole question of super priority versus a wage insurance scheme. That was an outstanding committee with representatives including the chairman of the committee, who was a former superintendent of bankruptcy and dean of law at

September 26, 1983
Bankruptcy Act
the University of Ottawa; Ron Lang, who was a member of the Canadian Congress staff; George Hitchman, who is the deputy chairman of the Bank of Nova Scotia; and Raymond Dufour, vice-president of a major bankruptcy firm. This committee, with broad representation from business, labour, the academic community and bankruptcy trustees, once again examined the relative merits of super priority versus a wage insurance scheme.
What was their conclusion? To no one's surprise, they said that super priority was clearly not the answer and that workers would not be protected by super priority. Instead, this committee again recommended the establishment of a wage earners' insurance scheme.
It is very rare that a committee with representatives from the CLC and the banking community agree on anything, but in this instance the committee was unanimous in saying that working people will be left out in the cold by super priority and that the only answer to giving equity in this area is the establishment of a wage insurance scheme. They recognize that some time would be needed in order to implement this recommendation and they suggested a three-year period in which the Consolidated Revenue Fund should ensure a super priority up to a maximum of $1,000.
We in this Party would be prepared to look at the possibility of some other interim solution, even including the possibility of a super priority for that limited period of time. How the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs or the Members of the Conservative Party in the House can possibly support a super priority which has been utterly discredited not only by their colleagues in the other place but by a non-partisan committee looking into this question certainly escapes me and, I am sure, those persons who are looking at this area of the law.
I will certainly look forward to the respresentations before the committee hopefully by Mr. Landry, who chaired the committee, by the CLC and many others who will graphically demonstrate that super priority is not in fact the answer. The answer must be the establishment of a wage insurance scheme such as those which have been in existence for some time in France, Germany and the United Kindgom. They have been operating successfully, I might add.
The other major area I would like to touch upon in conclusion is the question of the very difficult times which are facing farmers and the suggestion by the Government that it wishes to insert a provision in Bill C-12 to deal with the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. My Party and particularly the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), who has been in the forefront of efforts to ensure the passage of Bill C-653 as amended where necessary, are prepared to have that Bill passed forthwith. To suggest that farmers and workers should played off against one another in Bill C-12 is obviously completely unsatisfactory.
In conclusion, 1 look forward to the very serious concerns of the farming community and particularly the working people being brought before the committee for a very thorough and
comprehensive study. Change is certainly long overdue but we must ensure that that change is not merely cosmetic.

The Wage Earners Protection Fund would be self-sustaining and maintained by monthly contributions from all employers in Canada, based on the number of employees. Contributions from such a large number of employers would result in modest amounts being paid per employee. The only exception to this universal rule would be that no contributions would be required from employers with fewer than six employees.
That was the recommendation of the Senate Committee, that it should in fact be funded by employers. I also suggest that the Hon.
